title: Subnetting You Can Actually See

sources.title: RFC 4632 — Classless Inter-domain Routing
sources.notes: Section3.1: IPv4 prefix notation and address-block sizes including /24 and /26.

sources.title: RFC 3021 — 31-Bit Prefixes on IPv4 Point-to-Point Links
sources.notes: Section2.1: both addresses are interpreted as host addresses on /31 point-to-point links.

sources.title: RFC 1918 — Address Allocation for Private Internets
sources.notes: Private address range192.168.0.0/16; illustrative addresses are not global Internet destinations.

sections.title: One network, four smaller networks
sections.narration: This block contains 256 addresses. We want four separate networks, with no gaps and no overlap. How can a few extra bits create all four boundaries? Watch what happens when we move one dividing line.
sections.takeaway: Subnetting divides an existing address block into smaller prefix blocks.

sections.title: IPv4 addresses contain thirty-two bits
sections.narration: An IPv4 address contains thirty-two bits, displayed as four decimal octets. Each octet represents eight bits. The familiar dotted form makes the number readable, but the block structure becomes much clearer when we expose the bits underneath.
sections.takeaway: Dotted decimal is a readable way to write the underlying bits.

sections.title: A prefix marks the shared beginning
sections.narration: Slash twenty-four fixes the first twenty-four positions. The last eight may vary, so every address in this block shares the same beginning. A prefix describes that common part and tells us which remaining combinations belong together.
sections.takeaway: The prefix length counts leading network bits, not decimal digits.

sections.title: The mask expresses the boundary
sections.narration: A mask makes this boundary explicit: ones mark the fixed prefix positions; zeros mark the changing positions. For slash twenty-four, the mask is 255.255.255.0. The decimal form is simply another view of those thirty-two bits.
sections.takeaway: A contiguous subnet mask and its prefix length describe the same boundary.

sections.title: Find the network with bitwise AND
sections.narration: To extract the network, apply bitwise AND. A mask one keeps the address bit; a zero clears it. Applying this mask to 192.168.1.42 leaves 192.168.1.0. The variable part disappears, exposing the common prefix.
sections.takeaway: Masking an address identifies the prefix block that contains it.

sections.title: Count the parent block
sections.narration: Eight variable bits allow two to the power of eight combinations: 256 addresses. In the last octet, that's zero through 255. This counts every address in the block, before assigning any special network or broadcast roles.
sections.takeaway: Count all addresses before applying ordinary LAN host reservations.

sections.title: Borrow two bits for four subnets
sections.narration: Fix one more bit and the possibilities split in half. Fix a second and each half splits again. Four subnets require two extra prefix bits, moving our boundary from slash twenty-four to slash twenty-six.
sections.takeaway: Extending a prefix creates smaller blocks within the original block.

sections.title: Build the slash-twenty-six mask
sections.narration: The last octet of the new mask begins with two ones. Their values are 128 and sixty-four, totaling 192. Six zeros follow. That's why the complete slash-twenty-six mask becomes 255.255.255.192, rather than an arbitrary number to memorize.
sections.takeaway: Two leading ones in the last octet make the /26 boundary.

sections.title: Six host bits make sixty-four addresses
sections.narration: Six bits remain free inside each subnet. They produce sixty-four addresses. Four times sixty-four gives the original 256, which is a useful consistency check: moving the boundary divides the existing space without changing its total size.
sections.takeaway: The four /26 blocks exactly cover the original /24.

sections.title: The four binary prefixes
sections.narration: The two new subnet bits can be zero-zero, zero-one, one-zero, or one-one. With all host bits cleared, those prefixes begin at zero, sixty-four, 128, and 192. Four binary choices create four evenly spaced boundaries.
sections.takeaway: Aligned /26 network starts are separated by 64 addresses.

sections.title: Subnet one: zero through sixty-three
sections.narration: The first subnet covers last-octet values zero through sixty-three. On an ordinary LAN, zero identifies the network and sixty-three is broadcast. Hosts use one through sixty-two: sixty-two usable addresses within a sixty-four-address block.
sections.takeaway: Subnet one contains 64 total addresses and 62 ordinary host addresses.

sections.title: Subnet two: sixty-four through 127
sections.narration: The second subnet starts at sixty-four and ends at 127. Hosts occupy sixty-five through 126. Notice the broadcast ends in 127 here. Its identity comes from all host bits being one, not from always ending in 255.
sections.takeaway: Network and broadcast roles depend on the prefix, not just the last octet.

sections.title: Subnet three: 128 through 191
sections.narration: The third prefix begins at 128 and covers through 191. Its ordinary host range is 129 through 190. The calculation hasn't changed; the fixed subnet bits have moved us into the next group of sixty-four combinations.
sections.takeaway: Clear host bits while preserving the complete 26-bit network prefix.

sections.title: Subnet four: 192 through 255
sections.narration: The fourth block runs from 192 through 255, with hosts from 193 through 254. Together, the four ranges cover the parent exactly once. Their boundaries meet cleanly, and each address belongs to just one subnet.
sections.takeaway: Nonoverlapping contiguous ranges verify the subdivision.

sections.title: Locate the host ending in seventy
sections.narration: Where does seventy fit? Its binary last octet is 01000110. AND with 11000000 leaves 01000000: sixty-four. So 192.168.1.70 lies in 192.168.1.64 slash twenty-six. The mask finds the block directly, without searching a table.
sections.takeaway: A range check and a mask operation should identify the same subnet.

sections.title: Same prefix or a different subnet?
sections.narration: Seventy and one hundred share that sixty-four prefix. Address 130 belongs to the block starting at 128. Similar decimal addresses can cross a subnet boundary; masking both addresses reveals whether their network portions actually match.
sections.takeaway: Compare masked network prefixes, using the relevant mask.

sections.title: Remote destinations use a router
sections.narration: That boundary affects delivery. A host normally reaches a destination in its own subnet locally; another subnet needs a suitable next-hop router. This is a logical addressing decision, independent of whether the devices occupy different physical rooms.
bullets: Remote subnet: use a next-hop router
sections.takeaway: A gateway connects networks that have different prefixes.

sections.title: Choose a prefix for fifty hosts
sections.narration: Suppose the network needs fifty host addresses. Slash twenty-seven offers thirty usable addresses on an ordinary LAN, which isn't enough. Slash twenty-six offers sixty-two. Work backward from the required capacity to choose the smallest suitable block.
sections.takeaway: Choose enough host bits for the requirement and reserved addresses.

sections.title: More prefix bits, fewer addresses
sections.narration: Every extra fixed prefix bit halves the remaining combinations. Slash twenty-five gives 128 total addresses, slash twenty-six sixty-four, slash twenty-seven thirty-two. Longer prefixes mean smaller blocks because fewer positions remain free to change.
sections.takeaway: Every additional fixed bit halves the number of address combinations.

sections.title: The subtract-two rule has exceptions
sections.narration: Subtracting two is useful for ordinary LAN subnets, but isn't universal. Suitable slash-thirty-one point-to-point links can use both addresses; slash thirty-two identifies a single address. The address roles depend on the network's purpose and prefix.
sections.takeaway: The total-address formula is general; host usability depends on context.

sections.title: A subnet is not a security policy
sections.narration: A subnet boundary doesn't itself encrypt traffic or forbid crossing. Routing and access policies determine which communication is allowed. Splitting an address block organizes delivery; protection requires the relevant security mechanisms as well.
sections.takeaway: A prefix boundary does not replace a security policy.

sections.title: CIDR replaces the classful shortcut
sections.narration: Modern classless addressing uses the supplied prefix, rather than guessing a class from the first octet. Also, our 192.168.1 block uses private addresses. It illustrates internal network organization, rather than a globally routable public block.
sections.takeaway: Read the actual prefix instead of guessing an old default class.

sections.title: Check all four answers
sections.narration: Check the four starts: zero, sixty-four, 128, 192. Each broadcast sits one below the next boundary, ending at 255 for the last block. Equal block sizes and clean boundaries let us verify the entire split together.
bullets: Each ordinary LAN has 62 host slots
sections.takeaway: Verify alignment, size, boundaries, and coverage before assigning addresses.

sections.title: Move the boundary, solve the puzzle
sections.narration: Two bits created four prefixes; six remaining bits created sixty-four addresses per prefix. Masks, ranges, and host counts all follow from that same boundary. Once you see the division, the separate-looking rules become consequences of one picture.
sections.takeaway: Subnetting follows directly from fixed prefixes and variable address bits.
